name: Uma Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself and how you came to line work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: For fifteen years I ran the books and half the machinery on my in-laws' dairy farm. When Karl's father retired, none of us wanted to carry on with milk prices the way they were, so we sold, and our share left us well set. At 41 I started a line apprenticeship with the electricity company, because I'd always liked fixing things and I wanted a proper trade with a pension. I'm in my second year. Karl sells farm machinery at a dealer in town, and we've got Hanna, who's fifteen, and Jonas, who's twelve.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Our patch is hills and forest, so a lot of what we do is rebuilding lines after heavy snow brings trees down, and clearing round the lines before fire season. Henrik, our crew leader, is very particular, and he's right to be, because one mistake with a live line and you don't get a second. I'm good with the chainsaw and the machinery from the farm days, but slow and nervous on the technical work up the pole, and Piotr still has to talk me through the harder connections. I like the quiet up in the forest and the feeling of a job done right. What wears me out is the early winter mornings, and being the beginner again after years of running things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there we are, the world keeps turning. At the choir practice someone would bring it up and we'd all agree we never trusted it anyway. I don't post much, maybe a photo of the forest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means our choices hold. We sold the farm, I took up a trade, and it turns out that was sensible. I'd be content with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the apprenticeship and aim to qualify in two years. We'd keep the farm money split between savings and paying down the mortgage. I might use the AI thing a bit more for the paperwork, since it'd be harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AI Plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet morning after a storm, when the line's back up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might use AI more. How do you use it now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then, to check my spelling on job reports or help Jonas with his maths when I've forgotten how. Karl showed me after the dealership started using it. I treat it like a calculator, handy, but you still need to know roughly what the answer should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've seen farm machinery change a lot. Does that shape how you see this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very much. When the neighbours put in robot milkers, we laughed, and five years later we had one. So when people say nothing will change, I'm never quite sure.

S0.say: She'd say the world keeps turning and agree at choir practice that nobody trusted the hype anyway. She'd post a forest photo at most.
S0.think: She thinks it confirms that selling the farm and taking up a trade were sensible choices, and she'd be content.
S0.do: Keeps working towards qualifying in two years and keeps the farm money split between savings and the mortgage. Uses AI a little more for paperwork, since it would be harmless.
S0.feel: Calm, like a quiet morning after a storm when the line is back up.
S0.quote: When the neighbours put in robot milkers, we laughed, and five years later we had one.
S0.fieldNote: Uma's farm background makes her more realistic about automation than her calm suggests. She uses AI like a calculator and checks its work. Even in the plateau, she's not fully convinced nothing will change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change has always come, and the people who do well are the ones who learn properly and work hard. I'd say the company should keep training young people as apprentices and not just buy software. At church I'd say families need to help each other through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think line work is safe enough for years. Robots don't like snow on a forest slope. But Karl's job might change, because the dealership already sells tractors that drive themselves, and they need fewer salesmen when the machine sells itself online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify on time and pick up any new tool the company brings in, once Henrik and the others have tried it. I'd encourage Karl to look at the servicing side of the dealership, fixing the self-driving machines, rather than just selling. And we'd keep saving as we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing Steady Disruption?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A little watchful for Karl.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say any of that to Karl directly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already have, a bit. He gets defensive, says farmers still want a handshake. I think he's partly right, but I've seen how the young farmers buy things now, mostly on their phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Hanna and Jonas in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hanna's thinking about an apprenticeship as an electrician, which I'm very proud of. Jonas wants to be a vet. Both need a person with their hands, so I'd encourage them both.

S1.say: She'd say change always comes and those who learn properly and work hard do well. She'd want the company to keep training young apprentices, and tell her church that families should help each other.
S1.think: She thinks line work is safe for years because robots don't like snow on forest slopes. She worries more that Karl's sales job shrinks as self-driving tractors are sold online.
S1.do: Qualifies on time and picks up new company tools once her crew has tried them. Encourages Karl to move to the servicing side of the dealership, and keeps saving as before.
S1.feel: Calm, a little watchful for Karl.
S1.quote: Robots don't like snow on a forest slope.
S1.fieldNote: She values apprenticeship and family help over government schemes. Her worry focuses on Karl's sales job, where she's seen buying move online. She waits for her crew to try tools first, as she did with the robot milker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and families and churches will have to carry each other through it. I'd want the government to do something, but I'd rather it helped people find work than just handed out money. I wouldn't be marching, I'd be organising meals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. Two years means I'm barely qualified, Karl's job is gone, and robots that can climb poles in snow are coming. We'd be all right for money for a good while because of the farm sale, but I'd be 45 with nothing to do, and I'm not built for sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd sit with Karl and go through the money properly, and we'd stop the extra mortgage payments to keep cash close. I'd keep working every day until they replaced me. I'd talk to my sister, who's a carer, about whether there's work there, and I'd sit with Hanna about her electrician plans, because those might not be worth the years anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like hearing a chainsaw kick back, that half-second where you know it's going wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the not having time to try things. With the robot milker we had years of watching the neighbours first. Here there's no watching, it's just here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hanna about the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hardest one. I'd want to say do it anyway, a trade is never wasted, but I don't know if that's true anymore. I think I'd tell her to wait a year and see, and that would break my heart a little.

S2.say: She'd say families and churches will need to carry each other, and want government to help people find work rather than just hand out money. She'd organise meals rather than march.
S2.think: She'd be worried: barely qualified, Karl's job gone and pole-climbing robots coming. The farm money would cover them a good while, but she'd be 45 with nothing to do and isn't built for sitting still.
S2.do: Goes through the money with Karl and stops extra mortgage payments to keep cash close. Keeps working daily, asks her carer sister about work, and talks with Hanna about pausing her electrician apprenticeship plans.
S2.feel: Anxious, like the half-second of a chainsaw kicking back.
S2.quote: I think I'd tell her to wait a year and see, and that would break my heart a little.
S2.fieldNote: The steady habit of watching others first fails her here because there's no time to watch. Her cushion protects the money but not her sense of purpose. Advising Hanna against a trade would cut against everything she believes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get ready, and I'd tell people at church to start planning now and help each other. I'd say the company should keep training people right up to the end. I'd not make a great noise about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I qualify and get some good years in, and Karl has time to move to the servicing side. That's a lot better. At 48 I'd still need something, but I've started over once and I could again, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify on schedule and start using the AI tools more regularly, once everyone on the crew was using them, so I'm not left behind. We'd put any spare money onto the mortgage. And I'd look at what jobs around robots and machines need a person, maybe servicing them, since I've always been good with machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. Five years is like getting the forecast for a storm a few days ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you could start over slowly. What does slowly mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching first, like I always do. I'd see who on the crew moves into the robot side and how they get on, and then follow when I'm sure. I'm not the first one in, but I'm usually not the last either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Henrik, really. He's 59 and the best I've seen, and this job is his whole life. He'd be too young to stop and too proud to start again.

S3.say: She'd tell people at church to start planning and help each other, and say the company should keep training people right to the end, without making a great noise.
S3.think: She thinks five years lets her qualify and get some good years in while Karl moves to servicing. At 48 she'd still need something, but she's started over once and could again, slowly.
S3.do: Qualifies on schedule and uses AI tools more regularly once the crew does. Puts spare money on the mortgage and looks for machine-servicing work that still needs a person.
S3.feel: Uneasy but able to breathe, like getting a storm forecast a few days ahead.
S3.quote: I'm not the first one in, but I'm usually not the last either.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Uma fall back on her habit of watching and then following. Her machinery skills from the farm give her a believable path. She worries most about her crew leader Henrik.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and families, churches and companies all have a part to play. I'd keep saying the company should take on apprentices. I'd be calm about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd have eight good years as a lineworker, the kids through school and the mortgage nearly gone. I'd be 53, which is old enough that I might think about stopping early, given the farm money. Or I might move into servicing machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, work and save, and pay off the mortgage early. Around year five I'd do a course in machine maintenance, probably through the company. And I'd help Hanna and Jonas pick paths that still need people, like Jonas with his vet plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. Ten years is far enough off that most days I wouldn't think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned stopping early. Would you really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the robots are doing the line work by 2036 and we've paid off the house, I could spend more time with my mother, who'll be getting on by then. That wouldn't be the worst ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest thing the extra ten years gives you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to watch, which is how I like to do things. In two years I'd be thrown in. In ten, I can watch the neighbours put in the robot first, and then decide.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty of time and families, churches and companies all have a part to play, and keep pressing the company to take on apprentices. She'd be calm about it.
S4.think: She thinks ten years means eight good years on the lines, kids through school and a nearly paid-off mortgage. At 53 she might stop early thanks to the farm money, or move into servicing machines.
S4.do: Qualifies, works, saves and pays off the mortgage early. Takes a company machine-maintenance course around year five, and helps Hanna and Jonas pick paths that still need people.
S4.feel: Quietly uneasy, but it wouldn't cross her mind most days.
S4.quote: In ten, I can watch the neighbours put in the robot first, and then decide.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years suits her watch-then-follow style. Early retirement is a real option because of the farm sale, and she frames it around caring for her mother. She keeps returning to apprenticeships as the right way to bring people into work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to watch and learn, and it would hit Karl's job and mine and Hanna's plans all at once. What would help is the company keeping on and training the people it already has, and help finding real work rather than just money, with families and churches doing their part too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the young ones. Everybody talks about people like me, but it's the apprentices starting at eighteen I worry about. If nobody trains them, who'll know how to fix the robots when they break?

headlineQuote: If nobody trains them, who'll know how to fix the robots when they break?
portrait: Uma Fischer is a 43-year-old apprentice on a forest and hill line crew, after fifteen years running the books and machinery on her in-laws' dairy farm, whose sale left the family well set. She's a churchgoer who believes in apprenticeships and family help, uses AI now and then like a calculator, and likes to watch others try new things before following. Calm in the plateau and steady change, she worries most for her husband Karl's machinery sales job. AGI in two years makes her anxious because there'd be no time to watch, and she might have to tell her daughter to pause an electrician apprenticeship. With five or ten years she plans a slow move into machine servicing, or early retirement to care for her mother.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to watch and learn, and it would hit her job, Karl's job and Hanna's plans at once.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping on and training its existing people, help finding real work rather than just money, and families and churches doing their part.
